title: Unwanted effects and deterioration in therapy
summary: Therapy can have unwanted effects as well as benefits. This guide covers asking about them routinely, recognizing deterioration on measures, telling side effects apart from expected short-term discomfort, and what to do next.
whenToUse: At planned reviews, and whenever a measure total rises by a meaningful amount.
When starting a method known to bring short-term distress (for example exposure or trauma processing).
When a client reports new problems in relationships, work or wellbeing since starting therapy.

steps.heading: Explain in advance
steps.body: During informed consent, say that therapy can sometimes have unwanted effects, and that you want to hear about any.

steps.heading: Ask routinely
items: New or worse symptoms since starting.
Unpleasant memories or feelings that do not settle between sessions.
Strain in relationships, work or study linked to therapy.
Feeling dependent on therapy or the therapist, or feeling worse about themselves.
Anything about the therapy or therapist that felt unhelpful or hurtful.

steps.heading: Watch the trend
steps.body: When a GAD-7 or PHQ-9 total worsens by at least the meaningful-change amount shown in the trend tool and stays there, treat it as possible deterioration and review.

steps.heading: Sort out what is happening
items: Expected and temporary: distress during exposure that eases as planned.
Unwanted effect of therapy: a new problem caused by the treatment or how it was done.
Life events or illness unrelated to therapy.
Malpractice or boundary problems, which need a different response.

steps.heading: Act on it
items: Talk with the client and adjust the method, pace or focus.
Review the alliance and the formulation.
Consult or refer if the problem persists, and document what you did.

prompts: Sometimes therapy has effects people do not expect or want. Since we started, has anything got worse or felt unhelpful?
After our last session, did any memories or feelings stay with you more than you expected?
Your totals have gone up over the last few weeks. I want to take that seriously. What do you think is going on?
cautions: Do not dismiss every worsening as a necessary part of change.
Do not use a symptom rise alone to decide on risk; ask directly about safety.
Some practices are harmful and are never recommended, including conversion efforts and suggestive memory recovery techniques; see the legal and ethics hub.
Licensed side-effect questionnaires are link-outs only while their licenses are pending.
evidenceSummary: A 2014 review (Linden and Schermuly-Haupt) defines psychotherapy side effects and reports that unwanted effects are common but rarely assessed. A 2013 paper (Linden) distinguishes unwanted events from adverse treatment reactions and malpractice. A 2016 study (Rozental and colleagues) developed the Negative Effects Questionnaire for monitoring unwanted events. A 2018 meta-analysis of progress feedback (Lambert and colleagues) found that feedback reduced deterioration among clients who were not on track.
